newsitem.title: USA: Southwest Air moves to keep low-cost reputation.
newsitem.headline: Southwest Air moves to keep low-cost reputation.

text.p: Southwest Airlines, the original budget airline, said Thursday its costs were creeping up too quickly and announced a major cost-cutting programme to hold on to its position as the most efficient U.S. carrier.
Company executives said rising costs were to blame for a 10 percent drop in third quarter profits, and that a company-wide bid to make fresh savings was under way.

"We had been very much focused on growth over the past 5 years. Here, in '96, '97 and '98 we will be very, very focused on performing as efficiently as we can and driving our units costs hopefully down," Chief Financial Officer Gary Kelly said.

The carrier's effort will focus on using its purchasing muscle to push down the prices it pays suppliers, installing a new computer reservations system, introducing productivity initiatives in several operations areas and looking at ways of cutting the amount of fuel its planes burn.

Southwest's revenues grew rapidly from $1.31 billion in 1991 to $2.87 billion last year. Annual profits jumped from $26.9 million to $182.6 million and the fleet grew from 124 planes to 224 over the same period.
That growth continued in the first half of 1996 but the reimposition of a 10 percent sales tax, rising fuel prices and a jet fuel tax all hurt the carrier in the third quarter.

Net income for the three months ending Sept. 30 was $60.9 million, or 40 cents per share, down from $67.7 million, or 45 cents per share, in the same period last year. Operating costs per available seat mile rose 6.5 percent to 7.52 cents.
Kelly said at least half of the additional costs were due to the higher fuel prices and the fuel tax, but that a new emphasis on efficiency was clearly needed.

"We still have a very, very wide cost advantage over the rest of the industry. We just dont want to lose that. We don't want to get complacent over where we are, so we have a number of initiatives under way to arrest this trend," Kelly said.
He said the first phase of cost-cutting should bear fruit next year with annual savings of between $10 million and $20 million.

He stressed the cost-cutting programme would not be allowed to undermine Southwest's safety standards. "Obviously, safety is the No. 1 priority so in no way am I talking about taking measures that would impact safety," he said.

Southwest has not had a fatal accident in its 25-year history. It was the first U.S. budget carrier and has grown dramatically in recent years by sharply undercutting competitors as it has moved into new markets.
The airline earlier this year began services to Tampa, Ft. Lauderdale and Orlando in Florida and is to enter the Northeast on Sunday by opening services to Providence, RI.
Kelly said part of the increased costs in the third quarter were due to advance advertising costs associated with the new Providence service.
